claims.short_label: Secondary-reported 1893 'yeager' and 1894 'yeggs' tramp attestations (un-scanned external reports)
claims.statement: External scholarly reports cite tramp 'yeager' in the 23 January 1893 Hartford Courant (Green's) and 'yegg'/'yeggs' ('beg money') in the 14 January 1894 Cincinnati Enquirer (Grammarphobia), establishing pre-1900 tramp-beggar currency distinct from primary-scan safecracker attestations.
claims.rationale: Because both pre-1900 tramp-beggar citations (23 January 1893 Hartford Courant in Green's and 14 January 1894 Cincinnati Enquirer in Grammarphobia) rest on external scholarly transcriptions whose full-page public-domain newspaper scans are not yet hosted in DRAgNEt, the claim is graded 'partially_supported' pending direct masthead-scan collation.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Externally reported 1893-1894 newspaper evidence for 'yeager'/'yegg' in the intransitive/nominal tramp-beggar sense prior to documented safecracker specialization.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Independent primary-scan verification of the 1893 Hartford Courant or 1894 Cincinnati Enquirer pages within this repository, or safecracker specialization by 1894.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Full-page public-domain scans of the 1893 and 1894 issues remain to be collated directly into public/scans/yegg/.

limitations: CERT-1500-101, CERT-1500-102, and CERT-1500-107 rely on externally published scholarly citations rather than locally hosted page scans.
resolution_criteria: Collate full-page public-domain newspaper scans with visible masthead dates for the 23 January 1893 Hartford Courant and 14 January 1894 Cincinnati Enquirer into public/scans/yegg/.

claims.rationale: Primary ABA convention reports directly refute Pinkerton/press mythology linking the 1899 St. Paul incident to an eponymous safe-blower named John Yegg.

evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Internal unpublished Pinkerton agency case ledgers from late 1899 remain in archival collections.

limitations: ABA published summaries condense underlying Pinkerton operative reports.

claims.short_label: Proposed derivation from German Jäger / Pennsylvania German yagăr ('hunter') via 1890s tramp 'yeager/yegg'
claims.statement: Tramp 'yeager' (1893) -> 'yegg' (1894/1900) plausibly derives via apocope from German 'Jäger' / Pennsylvania German 'yagăr' ('hunter, forager'; cf. PG 'yawgă', 'ransack', Horne 1896, and Century 1909 '*yegger'), though secondary reinforcement from Scots/Shetland 'yagger' ('pedlar') or Anglo-Romani 'yag' ('fire') cannot be excluded.
claims.rationale: 1893 Hartford Courant 'yeager' and 1904 Reading Railroad 'John Yeager' lore point to Pennsylvania/Midwest German-English hobo contact before 1900 safecracker narrowing.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Documented phonological bridge ('Jäger'/'yagăr' -> 1893 'yeager' -> 1894 'yegg') and semantic plausibility in Pennsylvania-Midwest hobo foraging.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Direct documentary proof of apocope ('yeager' -> 'yegg') or the exact semantic shift from tramp beggar to nitroglycerin safe-blower.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Why 'yegg' narrowed abruptly from tramp begging (1894) to post-office safe-blowing (Jan 1900) remains undocumented.

limitations: Horne's Pennsylvania German 'yagăr'/'yawgă' scan is verified in the 1896 edition rather than an 1875 first-edition scan, and Rotwelsch dictionaries (Avé-Lallemant 1862) do not gloss 'Jäger' as 'safecracker'.
resolution_criteria: Verify original 1893-1899 Midwest/Pennsylvania hobo newspaper items linking 'yeager' and monosyllabic 'yegg' in the same camp or rail-line context.
Inspect a physical copy of Horne's 1875 first edition to confirm whether 'yagăr'/'yawgă' appeared identically in 1875.

evidence.reason: Supplies the 1893 'yeager' and 1894 'yegg' tramp-beggar chronological bridge.
Bounds Horne's Pennsylvania German Manual scan to its inspected 1896 Revised Edition.
Documents Pennsylvania German 'yagăr' ('hunter') and 'yawgă' ('ransack') in Horne (1896 ed.).
Documents the 1909 Century Dictionary Supplement reconstruction '*yegger, < G. jäger, hunter'.
Documents Shetland/Scots 'Yagger' ('pedlar, clandestine buyer') in Edmondston (1866) as a rival dialectal parallel.
Documents Anglo-Romani 'yag' ('fire') in Smart & Crofton (1875) as a possible safe-blowing reinforcement.

claims.case_section: Section 5: Rebuttal of Chinatown & Eponym Myths
claims.short_label: Rebuttal of Jack Black's 1926 Cantonese 'yekk' ('beggar') story and the 'John Yegg' safecracker myth
claims.statement: Jack Black's 1926 memoir claim that 'yegg' derived from a San Francisco Chinatown Cantonese word 'yekk' ('beggar') is contradicted by 19th-century Cantonese dictionaries (Williams 1856, Eitel 1877), and the 'John Yegg' safecracker eponym is uncorroborated in prison, ABA, and directory records.
claims.rationale: Cantonese beggar terms ('乞兒' hat1 ji4) bear no phonological resemblance to 'yekk', while 'yik' syllables denote unrelated morphemes ('change, wing, post').

evidence_boundary.establishes: Lexicographical refutation of the 1926 Cantonese 'yekk' = 'beggar' story and archival refutation of a historic safe-blower named 'John Yegg'.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Refutation of the separate Pennsylvania tramp surname 'Yeager' story (Popik & Cohen 1999).

limitations: Evaluates standard Guangzhou/Taishan Cantonese lexicons of the Gold Rush and Chinatown era.

evidence.reason: Demonstrates the 1899 St. Paul bank case involved sneak thief William Barrett, not a 'John Yegg'.
Confirms zero 'John Yegg' records across 1870-1905 directories and criminological texts.
Documents Jack Black's 1926 You Can't Win Chinatown 'yekk' ('beggar') origin claim.
Shows S. Wells Williams's 1856 Cantonese dictionary lacks any 'yekk'/'yik' noun meaning 'beggar'.
Shows Ernest John Eitel's 1877 Cantonese dictionary likewise lacks any 'yekk'/'yik' = 'beggar'.
Documents early conflicting 12 July 1903 Los Angeles Times 'John Yegg' folklore.
Confirms German Rotwelsch in Avé-Lallemant (1862) lacks an underworld 'Jäger' = 'safecracker' sense.
Confirms Leland's 1882 Romani vocabulary lacks a 'yegg' thief/beggar stem.
Shows Hotten (1874) 'Yack' denotes 'watch', unrelated to 'yegg'.
